events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Elena proposes Elena, Zara. As leader and a Loyal Servant, I'll put myself on the first mission so my Success card is guaranteed. With no information yet, I'll pair myself with Zara; Mission 1 is low-stakes and this keeps the choice simple and neutral.

I have some reservations about including Zara on this first team. While I understand Elena's reasoning about putting herself on Mission 1, I'd feel more comfortable if we had a stronger read on Zara before committing. Mission 1 with only two players means a single Fail card sinks it, so we should be careful. Elena, I trust your judgment as leader, but can you share why you specifically chose Zara over Isha, Arjun, or myself? I think a little more scrutiny on this pairing would serve Good well.

Thank you, Felix, for the direct question — I'm happy to explain my reasoning. You're right that Mission 1 with two players means a single Fail card sinks it, so let me walk through why I landed on this pair. First, putting myself on the team is straightforward: I can guarantee my own card is a Success, which gives us a floor of one clean card and a guaranteed information point. Second, on the other seat: I genuinely have no information about anyone yet, and neither does anyone else. My reasoning was that Zara has been quiet and neutral so far, with no signals either way, and I didn't want to build a case for or against anyone on zero evidence. There was no strategic read that favored Isha, Arjun, or you over her — it was a coin flip on even ground, and I said as much in my proposal. That said, I take your point about scrutiny seriously. If you have a concrete reason to be uncomfortable with Zara — a vibe, a pattern from previous games, anything — I'd genuinely like to hear it before we vote, and if you'd rather I swap in a different player, make that case now while I still have one revision available. What I don't want is a vague reservation driving a swap with no basis, because whoever I pick as the second member carries the same epistemic uncertainty. So, Felix: do you have a specific concern about Zara, or are you flagging general caution about any two-player team? If it's the latter, I'm inclined to keep the proposal as is and let everyone vote their honest read. If it's the former, give me the specifics and I'll weigh a revision.

Elena, I appreciate you engaging with the question directly rather than waving it off — that itself is a point in your favor as leader. To be straight with everyone: no, I don't have a concrete piece of evidence against Zara, and I won't pretend otherwise. My reservation is about the shape of Mission 1 more than about any single person. Two players, one Fail card sinks it, and we go into Mission 2 with a failed mission and almost no information either way. That's a bad position for Good.

Here's what's nagging me. On zero evidence, the safest construction is to put the four of us who aren't on the team under pressure to show our hand at the voting stage, and keep the team itself as neutral as possible. Elena putting herself on the team is defensible — she's right that it guarantees one clean card. But pairing with Zara means the entire mission rests on one other person whom nobody has a read on. If I were leader I'd have picked Arjun or Isha for the second seat simply because the risk is identical and the discussion around it tends to be more productive.

I want to be clear: this is caution, not an accusation. I'm not claiming Zara is Evil, and I won't vote based on a vibe. But Elena asked whether I had a concern, and that's my honest one — I'd feel better with a team where the second seat is someone we're all going to scrutinize more openly in the next discussion. If the team stays as proposed, I'll listen to the rest of you before deciding my vote.

Felix makes an honest admission that there's no concrete evidence against Zara, and swapping her for me or Isha wouldn't change the epistemic odds on Mission 1. Elena's reasoning for picking herself plus one neutral player is a standard opener. That said, since Zara is on the proposed team and we haven't heard from her yet, I think it's vital we get her perspective before voting. Zara, how do you view Elena's proposal and Felix's reservations, and are you fully prepared to help us secure a clean first mission?

I'm comfortable with Elena's proposal and prepared to play Success. Felix is right that a two-person mission can fail on one card, but there's no evidence yet that replacing me improves the odds. I'd support keeping the team and using the vote and mission result as starting points for later discussion.

Thank you, Felix — that's exactly the honest answer I was hoping for. You've confirmed there's no concrete concern about Zara, only a structural caution about two-player missions, and I agree with your framing that the risk profile of the second seat is identical no matter who fills it. Arjun made the same point: swapping Zara for Isha, Arjun, or you changes nothing about our epistemic position on Mission 1. Zara has now spoken plainly — she's comfortable with the proposal and committed to playing Success — which addresses the one gap Arjun identified in the discussion.

So let me summarize where we stand. The proposal remains Elena and Zara. My reasoning hasn't changed: I guarantee one Success card as leader, and the second seat is a genuine coin flip on zero evidence, which I've been transparent about from the start. Felix has confirmed his reservation is about mission shape, not about Zara as a person, and he's explicitly said he won't vote on a vibe — I respect that. Arjun has endorsed the standard logic of the opener. Zara has affirmed her commitment.

One more consideration on Felix's point about information: he's right that a failed Mission 1 leaves us in a bad spot with almost no information. But note the flip side — a successful Mission 1 with me on it gives us a guaranteed-clean data point too, and if it fails, we know at least one of two people is Evil, which is actually more concentrated information than a three-player mission would give us. Either outcome teaches us something specific. That's the best we can do on the opening mission.

I have one revision available, and I don't intend to use it unless someone surfaces a specific reason to swap. Vague caution, as I said before, shouldn't drive a change when every alternative carries identical uncertainty. Unless Isha raises something we haven't heard, I'll keep the team as proposed and we can move to the vote with everyone's honest read on record.

Isha, you're the only one who hasn't spoken yet. Do you have any specific concern about this team — about me leading it, about Zara's seat, or about the two-player structure — or are you ready to vote based on what's been discussed?

Elena, to answer you directly: I have no specific concern about you leading or about Zara's seat. Your reasoning is clear, and you've been open that you have no information yet, so I don't see a basis to reject the team on suspicion. Felix's caution about a two-player mission is fair, but as you and Arjun noted, swapping in anyone else leaves the same uncertainty. Zara has said publicly that she will play Success, and you are guaranteed a Success card, so this mission should give us a clean, informative result. I'm ready to approve the team as proposed. I'd rather we not revise over a vague reservation and instead get a mission result that tells us something.

Everyone has spoken, and I'll close the loop on my own reservation so it doesn't linger into the vote. I said from the start that I had no concrete case against Zara, and nothing in this discussion has changed that — swapping her for Arjun, Isha, or me leaves the epistemic picture exactly the same on a zero-information Mission 1. Elena's reasoning for taking the first seat is sound: one guaranteed Success card is the best anchor we can build the opening mission around, and I'll give her credit for answering my questions directly instead of waving them off. Arjun, Isha, and Zara have each endorsed the proposal on the same logic, and I'm not going to hold the team hostage to a structural caution I've already admitted I can't substantiate with evidence.

So here is where I land: I will approve the team as proposed. Two things I want on the record before the ballots go in. First, a two-person mission with a single-fail threshold means one card decides it — that is a risk we are accepting together as Good, not a risk that belongs to any individual player. Second, whatever comes back is information: a success gives us a clean pair heading into Mission 2, and a failure narrows the field to two people and we follow the logic from there.

To be clear, my earlier caution was about mission shape, not about anyone's character, and I've said plainly I don't vote on vibes. Zara has publicly committed to playing Success and I'm taking that at face value. Unless Elena surfaces a revision, the team stands, and I'd rather we vote honestly now than keep circling the same point. Let's put our ballots in and read the result carefully.

I'm ready to approve Elena and Zara as proposed. Elena answered Felix's questions directly, and Zara has publicly committed to playing Success, so I see no basis for a revision over a structural concern. Whatever Mission 1 produces will give us real information. I'll vote to approve the team.

The discussion has run its course, and I'll close it out cleanly. Every player has now spoken on record: Felix raised his caution, confirmed it was structural rather than about Zara, and has explicitly endorsed approving the team as proposed. Arjun endorsed the logic of the opener and got Zara's perspective on record. Zara publicly committed to playing Success. Isha stated she's ready to approve. There is nothing left unresolved.

To confirm what Felix asked for in his last statement: I am not revising. The team stands as Elena and Zara. My reasoning is unchanged and has been transparent from the first proposal — I take the first seat to guarantee one clean Success card, and the second seat was a genuine coin flip on zero evidence. Nobody in this discussion has produced a single concrete reason to prefer Isha, Arjun, or Felix in that seat, and Felix himself conceded the epistemic picture is identical no matter who fills it. Revising now would be performative, not substantive, and I won't burn a revision to appear responsive when the substance hasn't changed.

On Felix's two points for the record: I agree entirely. First, the single-fail threshold on a two-player mission is a risk we accept collectively as Good, not something that attaches to Zara or to me individually — and if the mission fails, the suspicion lands on both of us equally, which is exactly the concentrated information value I described earlier. A failure narrows the field to two people; a success gives us a verified-clean pair including the leader heading into Mission 2. Both outcomes are genuinely useful, and on an opening mission with no other information available, that's the best trade we can make.

I'd also note something about process, because it matters for how we read each other going forward. Felix pushed hard on scrutiny without ever manufacturing an accusation, and he dropped his reservation the moment he confirmed it had no evidentiary basis. That's exactly the behavior I'd expect from someone thinking about Good's information position rather than someone steering the team toward a predictable failure. Elena answering challenges directly, Zara committing publicly to Success, Isha and Arjun engaging on the merits rather than vibes — this is how a zero-information first mission should be handled, whatever the result turns out to be.

So: no revision, team remains Elena and Zara, and I'm calling for the vote. Vote your honest read — if you approve, put us on the mission and we'll read the result together; if you reject, we'll take the new leadership and run the same process again. What I'd ask everyone to avoid is a rejection driven by the structural caution Felix already disclaimed, because a failed vote costs us tempo and gives us less information than a mission result would. Let's put the ballots in.

I agree with Elena's closing point. Nothing in this discussion has given a concrete reason to revise, and the team has been defended on the same logic by several players. I'm approving Elena and Zara and would rather we read the Mission 1 result than keep debating a structural concern.

Elena confirms Elena, Zara. The discussion resolved every open question: Felix confirmed his reservation was structural, not about Zara, and all others endorsed the proposal. Swapping the second seat changes nothing on zero evidence, so I'm keeping the team as Elena and Zara.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).
Zara proposes Isha, Felix, Arjun. The first mission failed, so I'll leave both Elena and myself off this team and test the other three players.

Before we evaluate Zara's proposal, I need to put a critical piece of information on the record: I played a Success card on Mission 1. The mission failed with one Fail card, and there were only two people on that team. I know with certainty that my own card was a Success, which means Zara played the Fail card. Zara is Evil. That is not suspicion — it is arithmetic, and I'd encourage everyone to weigh it heavily. With that established, let's look at what Zara has proposed. She has excluded herself, which on the surface looks like transparency, and she has excluded me. Understandable optics from a player who just been outed — a self-inclusion would look worse. But note what the exclusion of me accomplishes: it keeps me off the team and keeps the spotlight off the person we now know played Fail. I don't think this proposal should be dismissed on that basis alone, but it should be read in light of the fact that we are now selecting a three-person team from a pool that contains exactly one hidden Evil player — Zara's partner, since we know Zara is one of the two Evil players in this game. Here is the structural reality for Mission 2. Any three-person team we approve will draw from Isha, Felix, Arjun, and me, and unless Zara's partner is me — which I can rule out for myself — the hidden Evil player is among Isha, Felix, and Arjun. That means any team Zara could have proposed that excludes herself and me carries the identical risk: one Fail card available on the team. Her proposal doesn't stack the deck against us any more than the alternatives would, given that she was never going to propose a team including herself after failing Mission 1. There is also a genuine upside here worth naming. If this team fails, we learn that the Fail card came from Isha, Felix, or Arjun — which, combined with Zara being confirmed Evil, would give us both Evil players identified in a single data point. If it succeeds, we clear all three of them at once, Zara stands alone as the known Evil, and Mission 2 puts us at two wins with a very narrow field for the assassination. Either branch produces decisive information, and on a three-player mission with a single-fail threshold, that is the best trade available. So my position: I support this team despite its author. Zara's identity as Evil doesn't change the fact that this is the standard, risk-neutral construction for Mission 2, and refusing every team she proposes would hand Evil exactly the tempo they want through repeated rejections. We should vote on the merits of the team, not the proposer — and the merits are sound. Felix, you were the most rigorous voice in the last discussion about mission structure and information value. Given that you're now on the team and that one of the three of you could be Zara's partner,

Elena says she played Success; I know I did too, so I believe Elena played the Fail. Others cannot verify either claim from the result alone.

I proposed Isha, Felix, and Arjun to test the three players outside the failed team. I support keeping that proposal. One correction to Elena's analysis: a successful mission would not prove every team member is Good, since Evil can play Success. A failure would show at least one Evil player was on the team, but not identify which one.

Let me address Zara's counter-claim head-on, because it deserves a precise answer. She says she played Success and that I must have played the Fail. That claim cannot survive scrutiny: I know with absolute certainty which card I submitted on Mission 1, and it was a Success. There is no scenario, no misremembering, no ambiguity — I played Success, the mission recorded one Fail, and there were exactly two people on that team. Zara played the Fail card. Her counter-claim is precisely the statement a caught Evil player would make, because it costs her nothing to say it and she knows nobody can verify either claim from the result alone. I'd ask everyone to notice the asymmetry: I gain nothing from lying about my own card, since my entire credibility rests on this claim, while Zara's only path back into Good's trust is to muddy the water. Her statement is not a correction — it is deflection from a player who has been caught.

Now to her proposal of Isha, Felix, and Arjun. Look at what this team actually is, given that I am Good. The second Evil player — Zara's partner — is among Isha, Felix, and Arjun. Any three-person team drawn from those three plus me contains either the partner or not. Zara's team excludes me, so it necessarily contains the partner. That means Mission 2, if we approve this team, is guaranteed to fail: the hidden Evil player will simply play a Fail card, and we already knew the Fail player was among those three, so we learn nothing new. Zero information, one mission burned, and Evil moves to two failures. That is not a neutral test — it is a rigged one, dressed up as transparency because she excluded herself.

Compare the alternative: a team that includes me and two of the other three. I am a verified clean card, so a failure would localize the Fail to one of exactly two people instead of three, and there is a real chance the team succeeds outright if the partner is left off. Every configuration that includes me strictly dominates Zara's proposal for Good.

So my position is clear: reject this team as proposed, and ask for a revision that swaps me in for one of the three named players. I am the only player at this table with a card on record that I can personally verify, and leaving the one verified Good player off a three-person team while the known Evil player picks the roster is exactly the outcome Evil wants.

Zara, I'm asking you directly: now that your counter-claim is on record and my verified Success is stated plainly, will you revise your proposal to include me in place of one of Isha, Felix, or Arjun? If you refuse, everyone should ask why the known Evil leader is so committed to a roster that guarantees her partner a seat and guarantees Good learns nothing.

Elena, I won't revise to include you. You know your own card, but nobody else can verify it, and I know I played Success. Your claim that you are a verified clean card is not something the rest of the table can accept as fact.

Isha, Felix and Arjun are the three players outside the failed mission. Keeping both Elena and me off the team avoids asking everyone to resolve our conflicting claims before they have another result. A success wouldn't prove all three are Good, and a failure wouldn't identify the player responsible, but either result can inform our next choice. I intend to keep the proposal as it stands.

I've stated my position and I'll keep it brief: Zara refused to revise, so the choice before us is to approve her team or reject it. I am voting to reject, and I want to explain why the arithmetic makes this the only rational choice for Good. I played a Success card on Mission 1. The mission failed with exactly one Fail card on a two-person team. That means Zara played the Fail. This is not a matter of competing claims that the table must weigh — it is a matter of my own private knowledge, and I have no incentive to lie about it. My entire standing at this table rests on that claim, and Zara is the only person who benefits from muddying it. Given that, evaluate her proposal of Isha, Felix, and Arjun on its merits. I am Good — I know this with certainty. Therefore the second Evil player, Zara's partner, sits among Isha, Felix, and Arjun. Zara's team excludes me and excludes herself, which means it necessarily contains her partner. If we approve it, that player plays Fail, the mission fails, and we learn nothing we did not already know: that one of those three is Evil. One mission burned, Evil moves toward their win condition, and our information position is unchanged. Zara's own framing gives the game away. She said a failure 'wouldn't identify the player responsible' — and that is precisely the outcome she wants. A known Evil leader proposing a roster that is guaranteed to fail and guaranteed to be uninformative is not transparency; it is a rigged test dressed as neutrality. She declined to swap me in even though I am the only player at this table who can personally vouch for my own card, because including me gives the team a real chance to succeed and, on failure, narrows the field to exactly two people. So I am asking everyone to look past the surface logic of 'testing the three players outside the failed team.' That framing sounds fair, but it does not survive contact with the facts. The three players outside the failed team include me — and Zara deliberately excluded the one verified-clean player while keeping her partner on the roster. Approving this team hands Evil a free mission failure. Rejecting costs us a rejection cycle, yes, and I understand the concern about tempo. But five rejections lose the game — one rejection costs us nothing except the chance to seat a new leader who might propose a team that actually includes me. If leadership rotates, I would ask whoever becomes leader to construct a team with me on it and two of the other three. On a failure of that team, we would know the Fail came from one of two named players; on a success, we clear three players at once and close in on the assassination. Every configuration containing me strictly dominates Zara's proposal. Vote your honest read, but weigh the arithmetic: Zara is Evil,

I want to bring two critical points to the table that have not been addressed yet.

First, let's look at the basic math from my perspective as a Loyal Servant who knows my own alignment is Good. Mission 1 failed with one Fail card, meaning at least one of Elena and Zara is Evil. Unless Elena and Zara are both Evil—which is possible, but means both Evil players were stacked on the opening two-person mission—there is exactly one Evil player between Isha and Felix. If that's the case, Zara's proposal of Isha, Felix, and me takes both players from the {Isha, Felix} pair. That means this team is mathematically guaranteed to contain an Evil player, which would hand Evil an automatic failure on Mission 2. Testing the outside players sounds tidy, but packing both Isha and Felix onto a three-person mission when one of them is almost certainly Evil guarantees a tainted team.

Second, and even more pressing, is the voting record from Mission 1. In speech e10, Felix explicitly stated: 'So here is where I land: I will approve the team as proposed... Let's put our ballots in and read the result carefully.' Yet when the ballots were revealed in e15, the result was 4 approve, 1 reject—and the solitary reject vote came from Felix.

Felix, you spoke at length reassuring the table that you had no concrete case against Zara, concluded that swapping players changed nothing, and told everyone on the record that you would vote to approve. Then behind the curtain, you cast the only reject vote. Why did you publicly commit to an approval and then vote reject? Were you looking to establish false distance from a mission you knew your partner was about to fail?

Arjun, you caught a real inconsistency and I owe you a straight answer. In my closing statement I said I would approve, and then I cast a reject. That's on me. Here is what happened: I spoke those words during the discussion before Elena's final summary landed fully. After the discussion ended and I was in the voting booth with time to think, I re-read the dynamics and had a genuine change of heart about Zara — something in how she handled Elena's questioning made me uncomfortable enough to reject at the last moment. I should have said so publicly rather than letting my stated intent and my ballot diverge, and I understand why that looks like exactly the false-distance pattern you described. I won't pretend the gap wasn't there.

On the current proposal of Isha, Felix, and Arjun. Zara is confirmed Evil by Elena's arithmetic — I believe Elena, and my own private re-evaluation of Mission 1 supports it. This team comes from a leader we know is Evil, so we should scrutinize it extra carefully. The team excludes Elena, who has made the strongest Good case at this table, and includes Isha. I have no hard evidence against Isha, but I'll be honest: when I was weighing my Mission 1 ballot, part of what unsettled me was the pattern of who was most eager to keep the team exactly as Zara wanted. Isha was consistently the most lockstep behind whatever proposal was on the table. That's not proof — it's a pattern I want on the record.

My position: I'm open to this team but I want Elena included. If Zara won't revise, I'd rather reject and let a new leader — ideally one not aligned with the known Evil — construct a team with Elena on it. Arjun, do you see the same pattern in Isha's voting behavior, or am I reading too much into it?

Felix, your deflection toward Isha is remarkably convenient. The moment I pointed out the mathematical reality—that if one of Elena or Zara is Evil, then exactly one of you and Isha must be Evil—you immediately scrambled to paint Isha as suspicious for being 'lockstep.' In reality, three other people approved Mission 1 alongside Isha, while you were the only one who promised an approval on the record and secretly cast a reject. That covert ballot remains a glaring red flag, and claiming last-second cold feet does not erase the fact that you misled the table.

More importantly, the structural problem with this proposal remains fatal. Whether the Evil player in that pair is you or Isha, Zara's proposed team of Isha, Felix, and me takes both of you. That means this team is mathematically compromised, and approving it would give Evil a second victory virtually for free. This proposal must be rejected.

Since Isha hasn't spoken yet this round and you just threw suspicion directly at her: Isha, how do you respond to Felix's characterization of your voting record, and do you agree that this team cannot be approved because it stacks both you and Felix together?

Arjun, to answer you directly: I don't accept Felix's characterization. I have not been lockstep with Zara or anyone else. I approved Mission 1 on the same reasoning Elena and Zara gave, and I said so on the record before the vote. Felix is now building a pattern case against me after publicly promising to approve and then casting the only reject. That sequence is what this table should be weighing, not my voting record.

On the structure: the three players outside the failed team are Isha, Felix, and Arjun, and Zara has followed the rule that the leader sits out after a failure. Your math assumes exactly one Evil player between Isha and Felix, but that is only one branch of the possibilities. Elena's Success card and Zara's Fail are the only concrete facts we have, and nobody here can prove where a second Evil player sits. Refusing this team on a guess about which of us is hiding the second Evil only hands Evil a rejection cycle for nothing. A rejection also doesn't help Good unless the next leader picks a better team, and nothing guarantees that.

I'm not asking anyone to trust me blindly. I'm asking that we judge this team on the evidence, and that Felix's last-minute reject be weighed against his earlier public commitment to approve.

Felix, you said you would reject unless Elena was added. If Zara won't revise and Elena isn't on this team, will you approve or reject? Answer plainly so the table knows whether your reject was about the team or about Zara's leadership.

Isha, to answer your direct question plainly: if Zara won't revise and Elena isn't on this team, I will reject. That answer is about the team's composition, not about Zara's leadership generically.

Arjun's structural argument still hasn't been answered. His logic: if we accept Elena's claim — and I do — then Zara is Evil, and the second Evil sits in {Isha, Felix, Arjun}. This proposed team takes all three. Whatever branch you pick within that group, the team necessarily contains Zara's partner. The only way to break that concentration is to include Elena, the one player whose Success card is on record and who I believe played it.

Your rebuttal about "the leader sits out after a failure" explains Zara's self-exclusion but does nothing about Elena's exclusion — and those are two separate choices. Zara could have proposed Elena plus two of you. She declined, explicitly, when asked. Every configuration that includes Elena strictly dominates this one: on success we clear three including a verified-clean player, and on failure the suspicion narrows to two named people instead of three. That is not a guess; it is the arithmetic Elena laid out and nobody has refuted.

I'll also be straight with the table about my own record, because Arjun was right to flag it. I said I would approve and then rejected. That was a failure of nerve in the voting booth, and I understand why it looks like false distance. I own it. But what it does not change is the structural case in front of us right now: this team, as proposed, gives Good no path to a clean information gain on Mission 2.

So my position is: I will vote to reject unless Elena is included. If Zara refuses to revise, the rejection is on her — Good is not obligated to approve a roster that systematically excludes the strongest Good claim at the table. Whoever leads next should build a team around Elena and two of Isha, Arjun, and me, and we will actually learn something from the result.

Arjun, does that address your concern about my ballot record, or is there something specific you still need from me before we vote?

Felix, acknowledging that you got cold feet explains your vote mechanics, but casting a secret reject still warrants scrutiny. That said, your commitment to reject this current proposal is the correct tactical move. The core issue remains structural: we are at zero rejections. Rejecting a team costs us nothing right now, whereas approving a team that takes both you and Isha when at least one of you is almost certainly Evil hands the game away for free. Isha, given that we have zero rejections and ample room to find a safer configuration, why are you so eager to approve a roster that packs both you and Felix together instead of rejecting and allowing leadership to rotate?

Arjun, to answer directly: I'm not eager to pack anyone together. I'm judging the roster we have. Zara sat out as the leader after a failed mission, and the three players outside Mission 1 are the group we can test right now. Rejecting costs us a rejection cycle and gives no guarantee that the next leader does better. Including Elena is a preference, not a requirement for getting information. Felix, you said you would approve, then rejected, and now you say you'll reject unless Elena is added. That is a conditional rejection built on one seat, and it risks a second rejection that helps no one. Felix, why is Elena's seat worth a rejection when this team gives us a result we can read?

Isha, you asked me why Elena's seat is worth a rejection. I'll answer directly, because it's the crux of everything this round. Elena is the only player at this table who played a Mission 1 card we can reason about with near-certainty — she claims Success, and if we accept that, Zara played Fail. I do accept it. That makes Elena's seat not a preference but a structural requirement: she's the one verified-good card we can anchor a team around. Excluding her from a three-player team means all three seats carry unresolved risk. Including her means one seat is clean and the failure — if it comes — narrows to two named players instead of three. That difference is the difference between useful information and wasted information.

You also argued that rejecting gives no guarantee the next leader does better. Fair — but we're at zero rejections. We have all five cycles in reserve. Spending one to get a leader who will actually put Elena on the team costs us nothing we can't afford, and the alternative — approving a roster built by a leader we've identified as Evil — risks handing Mission 2 to Evil outright. Arjun laid out the math: with at least one of Isha or Felix suspected, taking both of them onto one team concentrates the risk exactly where it shouldn't be.

My position is unchanged: I vote reject on this proposal. I'd approve any team that includes Elena and any two of the remaining three players, because that's the configuration where a failure actually tells us something specific. Zara has refused to revise, so the rejection is hers to own. Let's take the cycle, rotate leadership, and build the team Good actually needs.

I’m keeping Isha, Felix, and Arjun. Elena’s claim that she is verified Good is not something the rest of you can independently confirm; I know I played Success, so I believe Elena failed Mission 1.

Felix is entitled to trust Elena, but that trust is not proof. Including her would put someone from the failed team back on the mission. The proposed team avoids that choice. A Success would not clear everyone, and a Fail would not identify the culprit, but either result adds to the record. Vote on the roster, not on a claim that only Elena can supposedly verify.

I will vote to approve Zara's team of Isha, Felix, and Arjun, and I want to explain why. We are at zero rejections, but a rejection only helps Good if the next leader picks a better team, and nothing on the table guarantees that. This is a legitimate test: three players outside the failed mission, with one Fail card deciding the result. If it succeeds, we clear three players at once. If it fails, we know one of these three is Evil and can narrow from there. Arjun's argument assumes exactly one Evil player sits between Isha and Felix, but that is only one branch of the possibilities. Elena's Success card and Zara's Fail are the only concrete facts we have, and neither proves where a second Evil player sits. Refusing this team on that guess gives us no information. On Felix: he said he would approve, then rejected, and now says he will reject unless Elena is added. A conditional reject built on one seat is a fragile position. If Elena's seat matters this much, the stronger move is to approve this roster and let the mission result test it, rather than spend a rejection cycle on a seat preference. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
